content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work presents a method to implement the rejection option for a pre-trained classifier that estimates posterior class probabilities $P_{Y|X}$ (called soft-probabilities in the paper). The method does not require re-training the network. Experiments show the proposed method can achieve similar or better performances with respect to its competitors that usually require re-training or tuning.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strong points.**

The proposed method is neat, and can work with any classifiers that output $P_{\hat{Y}|X}$. It does not require re-training the network in order to add the rejection option. Experiments show the proposed method can achieve similar or better performances with respect to its competitors that usually require re-training or tuning.  

**Weak points.**

There are several serious issues, which I list below.

- Although the authors claimed that the proposed method is based on a sound mathematical framework and enjoy good properties, it is not (at least it is not accurate to claim so). Fundamentally speaking, a classier wants to abstain (or reject) when no class can be predicted confidently (i.e. $P(Y=y|X)$ is less than a threshold for all $y$), and this is usually achieved by assigning a cost for reject options (see Chow's rule). The cost will determine the threshold to be used for $P(Y=y|X)$. Yet, in this paper, it seems that the authors wanted to apply a threshold to $Pe(x) := 1 - P_{Y|X} (f_{D_n}(x)|x)$, the probability of classification error for a given classifier $f_{D_n}$. If so, this would contradict to the principle of reject options, in which whether to reject or not only depends on $P_{Y|X}$. Moreover, as the authors pointed out, $Pe(x)$ is usually unknown (since it depends on $P_{Y|X}$), so they used an upper bound of $Pe(x)$, $Gini(x)+\Delta(x)$ and applied the threshold to $Gini(x)$ in order to determine whether to reject. The problem is that, $\Delta(x)$ depends on $P_{Y|X}$ as well. But the authors simply ignored $\Delta(x)$ without any explanation.
- Although the authors claimed that the proposed method is free of hyper-parameters, it is not. The threshold parameter $\gamma$ needs tuning.
- The related work section is lengthy, but it does not make clear how the proposed method is related to the literature surveyed. Moreover, recent developments in reject options (e.g. [1] and [2]) were not discussed.

---
[1] 	Nontawat Charoenphakdee, Zhenghang Cui, Yivan Zhang, Masashi Sugiyama:
Classification with Rejection Based on Cost-sensitive Classification. ICML 2021: 1507-1517

[2] Chenri Ni, Nontawat Charoenphakdee, Junya Honda, Masashi Sugiyama:
On the Calibration of Multiclass Classification with Rejection. NeurIPS 2019: 2582-2592
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Overall I found the paper is not well-motivated. Its motivation is neither principled nor sound. Moreover, the paper is poorly written. The lengthy related work section did not address how the proposed method is related to the literature. The proposed method was not clearly explained, and several important details were not mentioned. The overall contribution is very limited. The reproducibility is okay, though.
content.summary_of_the_review: Based on the aforementioned, I think the paper needs substantial revisions to meet the standard. Therefore I vote to reject the paper.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work focuses on implementing the rejection option for a pre-trained classifier, i.e., enabling a classifier to know when to reject to give the answer for unconfident examples. This work shows that the Gini-impurity score can serve as a metric to make the rejection decision. The advantage of this score is that it is simple to implement and training-free. They provide empirical results on CIFAR-10/100, SVHN with ResNet and DenseNet architectures and demonstrate that this simple training-free method outperforms previous learning-based methods.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
It is a useful discovery to show that the gini impurity score can be used for misclassification detection, which outperforms previous learning-based methods. But I have a few concerns as follows.

A previous work (Wisdom of Committees: An Overlooked Approach To Faster and More Accurate Models ICLR 2022) demonstrates that a couple of other metrics are also a good confidence proxy and can be used for misclassification detection, e.g., maximum confidence, entropy, gap between top-2 logits/probabilities. These metrics are also simple and training-free. I think this work should compare to those metrics.

The above work applies the confidence metrics in the context of model cascades. It will be interesting to see similar results too (since knowing when to reject is not sufficient in practice and we usually need to resort to a more powerful classifier in this case).

Experiments are only provided on small benchmarks. Since most results are provided for image classification, it is strongly encouraged to show results on ImageNet especially the proposed method only needs pre-trained models and requires zero training.

It would be great to see results on more recent architectures too, e.g., EfficientNet, Vision Transformer, etc (there are a long list of pre-trained models available online, e.g., huggingface).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
This paper is well-written. Since the method is training-free, I believe it is easy to reproduce.

In terms of the novelty, due to the existing results in the previous work (Wisdom of Committees: An Overlooked Approach To Faster and More Accurate Models ICLR 2022), the findings in this work are not that surprising to me, unless the Gini-impurity score significantly outperforms those simple metrics.
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper provides a useful discovery and shows that Gini-impurity score can be used to measure the confidence of a classifier, based on which we can make rejection decision. But it is already known that  a couple of other simple metrics can also be used for the same role. I would like to see the comparison against those metrics to make the final decision. ImageNet results are also missing and it would be great to have them.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper is concerned with learning with abstention in the high target coverage regime ($\ge70\\%$). The authors adopt the post-hoc uncertainty calibration approach, as detailed in, e.g., Geifman & El-Yaniv 2017 . Specifically, the authors propose using the Gini impurty of the soft output of a pre-trained classifier as a score to determine uncertainty, and reject queries where this score is large, as determined by a threshold tuned using a held out validation dataset. It is empirically argued that this method is superior to prior state of the art methods on a variety of vision datasets and architectures.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strenghts: The questions of which post-hoc score to use in order to decide whether to reject a query or not, and how much performance one can pull out of these post-hoc scores, are both important, and relevant to the audience of this conference. The paper supplies a considerable empirical study to address these questions, and the results are quite valuable. The paper also gives an extensive background, which is appreciated.

Weaknesses: 

- Limited novelty: I think that this paper is far too incremental. The basic idea of using a post-hoc uncertainty score on the soft output of a pre-trained classifier to decide whether to reject a query or not is _very, very_ well established. Given this, the only methodological contribution of this paper is to say that one should use the Gini score! 

- Further, perhaps egregiously, the use of this particular score over any other is not meaningfully justified! Indeed, why should one use the Gini score (which boils down to the $\chi^2$-divergence between $\hat{p}(y|x)$ and the uniform), and not one based on some other $f$-divergence? What makes this particular score so much better? For that matter, what is the performance of just using the max-entropy here? I think there is indeed an interesting question here (which post-hoc score to use for rejection), but the paper does not get anywhere close to studying it.
     - Apropos of this, I want to mention that the development of section 3.2 is entirely unconvincing - main term of the upper bound is $\mathrm{Gini}$ and that of the lower bound is $\sqrt{\mathrm{Gini}}$, and so unless the $\mathrm{Gini} \approx 1,$ the bounds are not tightly characterising the probability of error; further, the error term is the KL divergence between the true and estimated posteriors - why is this well controlled for most points in the dataset? (I understand that this argument is made in the DOCTOR paper, but it's equally unconvincing there). 
    - In a similar vein, the DOCTOR paper is ultimately only comparing to temperature scaled entropic scores - I don't find it particularly authoritative in its treatement of Gini, and certainly not in why Gini is the best idea for selective classification (which ultimately is a related but distinct problem from error prediction).

- One interesting observation of the paper is that the simple post-hoc calibration method does nearly as well (or indeed better) than more sophisticated methods such as selective net. Unfortunately this observation is comparing to an out of date set of procedures - since 2019, improvements have been made in the state of the art on selective classification, including Gangrade et al., and Rabanser et al. - these need to be compared to! If the point is to say that the simple post-hoc methods work as well as extensively trained models, then the improved training methods certainly need to be accounted for. Note also that the small or no advantage of these prior methods has previously been noted in the literature - e.g. Gangrade et al. make this point on the resnet architecture.

- Finally, the paper concentrates entirely on the high target coverage regime. However, this is not the only use case of selective classification (e.g. the high target accuracy regime is critical to using SC for inference time resource trade-offs, see Gangrade et al. 2021). A more complete answer to the question of whether post-hoc scores are good enough would need to take this regime into account as well. As such, in my opinion the story of the paper is incomplete until a comparable study of this setting is done.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The paper is clearly written, and the methods and approach are easy to follow. The empirical evaluation is extensive, and does demonstrate fairly well that the post-hoc method proposed does nearly as well or better than the methods compared to. I believe that the results should be reproducible, since the method is simple and well specified. I do question the novelty of the paper, as discussed previously.

Comment: I find it odd that standard deviations over just five trials are reported - why do the means concentrate well enough that this is a reasonable error estimate? I think with just five seed (which is understandable due to the computational burden of the problem), just reporting the range is far more representative than the standard deviation. Relatedly, I find the bolding of results to indicate which is best somewhat suspect - at the very least if the mean $\pm$ standard dev intervals overlap, then (due to the small sample size) one cannot reasonably declare one method to be better than the other. This happens repeatedly across Table 1. Note that the point that post-hoc methods are good enough would be equally well made if multiple entries in the table are bolded.
content.summary_of_the_review: On the whole I think the paper is getting at interesting questions, but presents a far from convincing answer to them. The simple contribution of using Gini as a post-hoc score is in my opinion of limited novelty, and does not provide enough of a contribution to bolster the above incomplete study. As such, I recommend rejecting the submission.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
